section: What are we going to build?
text:
What are we going to build?



Primary (essential) hypertension
Condition-based phenotype

Start with hypertension codelist
Create initial base cohort
Require ≥ 180 days prior observation

Restrict to adults (≥ 18 years)

Require a second hypertension record within 365 days
Exit at end of observation





Warfarin users
Drug-based phenotype

Start with warfarin codelist
Create initial exposure cohort
Require ≥ 365 days prior observation

Collapse exposures with a ≤ 30-day gap

Require 365-day washout

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
CodelistGenerator

The CodelistGenerator R package provides tools to


Explore OMOP CDM vocabularies available in the database
Generate codelists systematically using vocabulary-based search strategies
Generate codelist diagnostics to assess code use and identify potentially missing concepts

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Generating candidate concepts
Today, we’ll focus on the getCandidateCodes() function to identify candidate concepts for our two phenotypes.

getCandidateCodes(
  cdm,
  keywords,
  exclude = NULL,
  domains = "Condition",
  vocabularyId = NULL,
  standardConcept = "Standard",
  searchInSynonyms = FALSE,
  searchNonStandard = FALSE,
  includeDescendants = TRUE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE
)


The function returns candidate concepts for review, together with the search strategy used to identify them.
This allows us to define a systematic and reproducible codelist search strategy.

Primary hypertension codelist







Note


A refined search strategy does not mean we have a final codelist.
CodelistGenerator helps us define a reproducible search strategy and generate a preliminary codelist.
Before cohort construction, this preliminary codelist is clinically reviewed.
Once cohorts are created, diagnostics provide further evidence to support additional codelist review and refinement.

Primary hypertension cohort

We will progressively apply our cohort inclusion criteria to identify adults with primary (essential) hypertension.

Create a base cohort from our essential hypertension codelist
Keep the first qualifying entry

Restrict to age ≥ 18 years

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Warfarin cohort
→ Create treatment episodes and identify new users
We now combine nearby exposures into treatment episodes and apply our new-user criteria:

cdm$warfarin_new_users <- cdm$warfarin_base |>

  # Collapse exposures separated by ≤30 days
  collapseCohorts(
    gap = 30,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # Require ≥365 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    minPriorObservation = 365,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # No warfarin exposure during the previous 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "warfarin_base",
    window = c(-365, -1),
    intersections = 0,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  )

PhenotypeR
PhenotypeR provides a standardised set of diagnostics to review and evaluate phenotypes created using the OMOP CDM.







Database diagnostics

databaseDiagnostics()








Codelist diagnostics

codelistDiagnostics()






Cohort diagnostics

cohortDiagnostics()

populationDiagnostics()

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Database Diagnostics
Summarise the database metadata including:

Snapshot
Summary of the person table

Summary of the observation period

Summary of the clinical tables (e.g., condition_occurrence) where concepts from the codelists defining the cohorts are found.









Note








Database diagnostics use functionality from OmopSketch.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Codelist Diagnostics

Summarise the codelist associated with your cohort including:


Achilles codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)

Orphan codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)
Cohort code use

Measurement code use (only if measurement concepts are present in your codelist)

Drug diagnostics (only if drug concepts are present in your codelist)










Note








Codelist diagnostics use functionality from CodelistGenerator to evaluate the use of concepts from our codelists in the OMOP CDM.
If the codelists contain measurement concepts, MeasurementDiagnostics is used to evaluate those concepts.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text: Cohort Diagnostics

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Cohort Diagnostics
Summarise and evaluate the cohorts including:

Cohort count & attrition

Cohort characteristics — Baseline characteristics of the cohort

Large-scale characteristics — Clinical records observed in different time windows

Compare cohorts — Overlap and timing between cohorts (if multiple cohorts)


Cohort survival — Survival until death (if death table is available)










Note








Cohort diagnostics use functionality from CohortCharacteristics to characterise and compare cohorts, and CohortSurvival to perform survival analyses.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Population Diagnostics

Contextualises the frequency of your study cohorts in the database calculating:

Incidence
Period Prevalence










Note








Population diagnostics use functionality from IncidencePrevalence to estimate the incidence and prevalence of our cohorts in the database population.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Run diagnostics together
Rather than running each diagnostic separately, phenotypeDiagnostics() allows us to run them together.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(),
  populationDiagnostics = list()
)


We can choose which diagnostics to run and customise their parameters.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(
    cohortSample = 1000
  ),
  populationDiagnostics = NULL
)

  cdm$warfarin_new_users,
  name = "phenotypes"
)
cdm$phenotypes |> settings()

title: Using LLMs for phenotyping
text:
Caveats
I will be showing you what you can do, not what you should do

Approaches shown today may be out of date by next week/month/year


Creating LLM tooling for phenotyping is easy, creating LLM tooling that improves the quality of research and provides a good user experience is hard


Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, for which task.


System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.


Closed-weight models often show performance drift, making validation even harder.

title: Using LLMs for phenotyping
text:
More caveats
Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Antrhropic, etc)

And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources)

title: Using LLMs for phenotyping
text:
Even more caveats
Low quality health research is prevalent

Reproducibility crisis in health research


Impact of increased LLM adoption? Double-checking and adding context vs unreproducible black box ….

title: Using LLMs for phenotyping
text:
Unstructured chat

# chat_qwen$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension")


chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension")

Hypertension encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations. Key features 
include:

*   **Elevated Blood Pressure:** Defined by consistent systolic (≥140 mmHg) or 
diastolic (≥90 mmHg) readings on multiple occasions.
*   **Signs & Symptoms:**
    *   **Asymptomatic:** Often discovered during routine blood pressure 
monitoring.
    *   **Headaches, Dizziness, Blurred Vision:** Suggestive of elevated 
intracranial pressure.
    *   **Chest Pain, Shortness of Breath, Palpitations:** May indicate 
cardiovascular complications.
    *   **Nosebleeds, Hematuria:** Can be associated with underlying vascular 
disease.
    *   **Annoyance, Irritability:** Non specific signs of poorly controlled 
BP.
*   **Risk Factors:** Family history, age, race, obesity, sodium intake, 
physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, and certain medications 
(e.g., NSAIDs, corticosteroids) can contribute.
*   **Comorbidities:** Diabetes, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, and 
metabolic syndrome often coexist.

The clinical presentation varies widely, with some individuals presenting with 
overt symptoms while others remain asymptomatic. A comprehensive assessment, 
including blood pressure measurement, clinical examination, and consideration 
of risk factors, is crucial for accurate diagnosis and management.

Structured chat
Remember, even with the same model you can get different results!

chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama(
  model = "MedGemma:4b", 
  system_prompt = prompt
)
expected_age <- NULL

      ),
      average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer(

  cli::cli_inform(

$hypertension$introduction_synonyms
[1] "Hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure. Other terms used include High Blood Pressure (HBP) and Hypertenion. It is a significant public health concern worldwide."

$hypertension$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms
[1] "Hypertension is often asymptomatic, with many individuals unaware they have it until complications arise. When symptoms are present, they may include severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, anxiety, confusion, and vision problems. These symptoms are often associated with severely elevated blood pressure."

$hypertension$epidemiology
[1] "Hypertension prevalence increases with age. It is more common in men than women, but the gap is narrowing. Risk factors include obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, excessive alcohol consumption, smoking, and family history. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, sex, and race. Comorbidities associated with hypertension include cardiovascular disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. It is also a significant risk factor for heart disease and stroke."

$hypertension$assessment_diagnosis
[1] "Diagnosis is based on repeated blood pressure measurements at the healthcare provider's office or other healthcare setting, ideally at the upper end of normal range to ensure accurate assessment. The average of multiple readings is used for diagnosis. Other tests are not routinely required for diagnosis unless there are symptoms that cause concerns."

$hypertension$therapeutic_plan_treatment
[1] "The initial treatment plan for hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes (such as a low-sodium diet) and regular exercise. If lifestyle changes are insufficient, medication is often prescribed. Common medications include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), diuretics, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers. The choice of medication depends on the individual patient's characteristics, including age, race, other medical conditions, and potential side effects. The goal of treatment is to reduce blood pressure to a target level, usually below 140/90 mmHg."

$hypertension$complications_prognosis
[1] "Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular disease (such as heart attack and heart failure), stroke, chronic kidney disease, and vision loss. The prognosis for patients with hypertension depends on the severity of the condition, the presence of complications, and adherence to treatment. Early diagnosis and aggressive management of hypertension can significantly reduce the risk of these complications."

$hypertension$disqualifiers
[1] "Conditions that might mimic the symptoms of hypertension, or cause a similar presentation in patient’s might be considered alongside the initial diagnosis, and might be treated as separate diseases. These include heart failure, pheochromocytoma, and renal artery stenosis. These conditions are considered alongside the initial diagnosis but are then differentiated by other tests."
